stem: After running `dbt run`, a developer sees `Compilation Error in model src_listings (models/src/src_listings.sql) 'listings' is undefined`, pointing at a `{{ ref('listings') }}` call where no model named `listings` actually exists in the project. The team needs the fastest documented fix. What should they do?

option_texts.A: Open the file the error names, search for the misspelled reference, and correct it to the actual model's file name
option_texts.B: Run `dbt deps`, since an undefined reference always means a missing package dependency
option_texts.C: Add a `source()` block for `listings`, since any undefined `ref()` should be converted to a source
option_texts.D: Ignore it; an undefined reference to a nonexistent model resolves automatically to the closest matching name

drill_answer_short: An undefined ref() name means the referenced model doesn't exist; fix the reference to the real model name
decision_hinge: Model 'model.jaffle_shop.customers' (models/customers.sql) depends on a node named 'stg_customer' which was not found. There must be a file named stg_customer.sql for this to work. Replace this reference with a reference to another model, in this case stg_customers.

plausible_options.B: no model named `listings` actually exists in the project

eliminated_by.C: where no model named `listings` actually exists in the project
eliminated_by.D: where no model named `listings` actually exists in the project

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a missing package macro is a different failure than a ref() pointing at a nonexistent model
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — dbt gives no rule for silently converting an undefined ref() into a source() call
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt never auto-resolves an undefined reference to the nearest matching name

stem: A production run fails with `Database Error in model dim_listings_cleansed (models/dim/dim_listings_cleansed.sql) 001003 (42000): SQL compilation error: syntax error line 14`, and the model's Jinja and YAML had already parsed successfully earlier in the same run. The team needs to know which step of dbt's process actually produced this error. Which step is it?

option_texts.A: SQL execution, since the warehouse rejected the compiled SQL it was sent, after Jinja and YAML had already parsed
option_texts.B: Parsing, since a syntax error always means the Jinja template itself already failed before anything parsed cleanly
option_texts.C: Graph validation, since a dependency cycle often shows up as a warehouse error code during that step
option_texts.D: Initialize, since the connection check must have failed before this specific model could even be selected

drill_answer_short: A warehouse-reported syntax error at a specific line is a Database Error, at the SQL execution stage
decision_hinge: SQL execution: Run the models -- Database Error. Database Errors come from your data warehouse, and dbt passes the message on.

plausible_options.B: the model's Jinja and YAML had already parsed successfully earlier in the same run

eliminated_by.C: the model's Jinja and YAML had already parsed successfully earlier in the same run
eliminated_by.D: the model's Jinja and YAML had already parsed successfully earlier in the same run

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — a syntax error reported by the warehouse happens at SQL execution, a later step than parsing Jinja templates
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — a numbered error code here comes from the warehouse's own SQL engine, not dbt's graph-cycle check
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — the error names a specific model and line, which requires the project to already be initialized and connected

stem: A developer runs `dbt compile` and sees `Compilation Error Could not find a match for macro 'dbt_utils.surrogate_key' in any installed packages`, even though `packages.yml` lists `dbt-labs/dbt_utils`. The team needs the most likely cause and fix, before assuming the macro name itself is wrong. What should they check first?

option_texts.A: Whether `dbt deps` has actually been run since the package was added; package macros only become available after dbt pulls the dependency into `dbt_packages`
option_texts.B: Whether the project's dbt version is too old to support any third-party packages at all
option_texts.C: Whether the macro needs to be manually copied from GitHub into the `macros/` folder, since packages do not expose macros directly
option_texts.D: Whether `profiles.yml` lists the correct target, since package macros resolve per target environment

drill_answer_short: Package macros are unavailable until dbt deps has actually pulled the package into dbt_packages
decision_hinge: dbt deps pulls the most recent version of the dependencies listed in your packages.yml from git. Run dbt deps to install the package(s). Packages get installed in the dbt_packages directory.

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — third-party package support is a standard dbt feature, not something a newer dbt version unlocks
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a correctly installed package exposes its macros automatically, with no manual copying required
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — package macro availability is not tied to which profiles.yml target is active

stem: Running `dbt run` produces `Encountered an error: Found a cycle: model.airbnb.dim_listings_cleansed --> model.airbnb.fct_reviews --> model.airbnb.dim_listings_cleansed`. The team needs the correct fix, since neither model can be dropped. What should they do?

option_texts.A: Update the `ref()` calls so the two models no longer depend on each other, breaking the cycle in the DAG
option_texts.B: Add `{{ this }}` to one of the `ref()` calls, which lets dbt resolve mutual dependencies without breaking the cycle
option_texts.C: Increase `--threads` so dbt can build both models concurrently instead of resolving a strict build order
option_texts.D: Rename one of the two models, since dbt treats identically-structured model names as the cause of dependency cycles

drill_answer_short: A cycle must be broken by removing one of the mutual ref() dependencies
decision_hinge: Your dbt DAG is not acyclic, and needs to be fixed. Update the ref functions to break the cycle. If you need to reference the current model, use the {{ this }} variable instead.

plausible_options.C: since neither model can be dropped

B.signal: since neither model can be dropped
B.requires_fact: Update the ref functions to break the cycle; the this variable is for referencing the current model's own relation, not for resolving mutual dependencies between two separate models.

eliminated_by.D: since neither model can be dropped

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — this refers to the current model itself, it does not let two separate models keep referencing each other
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — thread count controls parallelism, it has no effect on whether the DAG itself is acyclic
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt detects cycles from ref() dependencies, not from name similarity

stem: A developer runs `dbt run --select fct_reviews` on a brand-new CI schema. `fct_reviews` references an ephemeral model, which in turn selects from a raw table using `source()`. The build fails because that raw table does not exist anywhere the CI run can reach. The team needs to know what actually must exist for this build to succeed, given that the ephemeral model never creates a database object of its own. What's the real requirement?

option_texts.A: The raw table named under the source() call must already be populated somewhere this run can reach, since dbt never builds source tables itself
option_texts.B: The ephemeral model must first be built as its own standalone object before the downstream model can select from it
option_texts.C: Nothing extra is required; an ephemeral dependency is skipped entirely when building on a brand-new schema
option_texts.D: A `--full-refresh` flag is required before any source can be read for the first time on a new schema

drill_answer_short: A source table is raw data dbt never creates; it must already exist wherever the run points
decision_hinge: Sources make it possible to name and describe the data loaded into your warehouse by your Extract and Load tools. dbt does not build source tables; they must already exist.

plausible_options.B: that raw table does not exist anywhere the CI run can reach

C.signal: given that the ephemeral model never creates a database object of its own
C.requires_fact: dbt interpolates the code from this model into dependent models using a common table expression; it is not built directly into the database.

eliminated_by.D: that raw table does not exist anywhere the CI run can reach

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — an ephemeral model is never built as a standalone object; its SQL is injected as a CTE wherever referenced
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated fact — an ephemeral model's logic still runs, interpolated into the referencing model, it is not skipped
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — --full-refresh rebuilds incremental models; it has no bearing on whether a raw source table exists

stem: Running `dbt parse` on a `sources.yml` file fails with a YAML parsing error referencing a specific line number, and the file's `tables:` list entries are indented inconsistently with the rest of the block. The team needs to know the most likely category of mistake behind this, before guessing at an unrelated config fix. What's the likely cause?

option_texts.A: Indentation: inconsistent spacing means the YAML parser itself cannot turn the file into a valid dictionary
option_texts.B: An unrecognized top-level property, the same category of error as an unexpected config key
option_texts.C: A missing `source()` call somewhere else in the project referencing this file
option_texts.D: A Jinja tag inside the sources file that was never closed

drill_answer_short: A YAML parse error pointing at a line number is usually an indentation problem
decision_hinge: dbt wasn't able to turn your YAML into a valid dictionary. Usually, it's to do with indentation -- here's the offending YAML that caused this error.

plausible_options.B: The team needs to know the most likely category of mistake behind this

eliminated_by.C: the file's `tables:` list entries are indented inconsistently with the rest of the block
eliminated_by.D: the file's `tables:` list entries are indented inconsistently with the rest of the block

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — an unrecognized key is a structurally valid file with a wrong key, a separate error from this one
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a missing source() call elsewhere would not cause a YAML parsing error inside this specific file
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — sources.yml contains no Jinja tags that need closing

stem: A model runs successfully in the `DEV` schema but fails in production with `Database Error in model dim_listings_w_hosts Insufficient privileges to operate on schema 'AIRBNB_PROD'`. The team needs to identify which step of dbt's process actually failed here, and what the real cause is. What's going on?

option_texts.A: A rejection at the SQL execution step; the production role lacks the grants needed to create or modify objects in that schema
option_texts.B: A Compilation Error, because the model's Jinja must reference an invalid schema name string in production
option_texts.C: A Dependency Error, since a permissions message always indicates a missing upstream model
option_texts.D: A Runtime Error, because dbt could not even connect to the warehouse at all in this environment

drill_answer_short: A warehouse permission rejection at build time is a Database Error, not a compile or connection failure
decision_hinge: SQL execution: Run the models -- Database Error. Database Errors come from your data warehouse, and dbt passes the message on; you may need to work with a DBA to confirm access.

plausible_options.B: fails in production with `Database Error in model dim_listings_w_hosts Insufficient privileges to operate on schema 'AIRBNB_PROD'`

eliminated_by.C: runs successfully in the `DEV` schema but fails in production
eliminated_by.D: runs successfully in the `DEV` schema but fails in production

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — the error is explicitly labeled a Database Error, a later stage than Jinja/YAML parsing
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — insufficient privileges is a permissions issue, unrelated to a missing upstream dependency
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — the model successfully ran in DEV and the error names a specific schema permission issue, implying the connection itself succeeded

stem: An incremental model is configured with `on_schema_change='append_new_columns'`. A developer adds a new nullable column to the model's SQL. After the next incremental run, the new column exists in the target table, but the team needs to know what value it holds for rows already present before this change. What's the actual outcome?

option_texts.A: Existing rows get `NULL`; none of dbt's schema-change behaviors backfill values into old records for a newly added column
option_texts.B: Existing rows are automatically backfilled by re-running the new column's logic against all historical data
option_texts.C: The entire table is silently rebuilt from scratch the next time the model runs, as if `--full-refresh` had been passed
option_texts.D: The build fails, because `append_new_columns` only allows new columns on brand-new rows, not existing tables

drill_answer_short: append_new_columns adds the column but never backfills historical rows; they get NULL
decision_hinge: None of the on_schema_change behaviors backfill values in old records for newly added columns. If you need to populate those values, we recommend running manual updates, or triggering a --full-refresh.

plausible_options.C: the new column exists in the target table, but the team needs to know what value it holds for rows already present before this change

B.signal: the new column exists in the target table, but the team needs to know what value it holds for rows already present
B.requires_fact: None of the on_schema_change behaviors backfill values in old records for newly added columns; to populate those values you must run manual updates or trigger a full refresh yourself.

eliminated_by.D: After the next incremental run, the new column exists in the target table

distractor_traps.B: T4: breaks a stated fact — none of the on_schema_change behaviors backfill old records automatically
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — append_new_columns explicitly avoids a full rebuild; a silent rebuild is not its documented behavior
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — the stem says the column already exists in the table after the run, so the build did not fail
